title: El Viaje de Evita — de Los Toldos a la Recoleta, y la odisea del cuerpo
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: La Hija Natural de la Pampa

stops.name: Los Toldos — la casa prestada en la pampa
stops.campa: On the flat pampa where the Coliqueo tolderías once stood, in a house lent to the family because the father's blood is not theirs to give, María Eva is born — the fifth and last child of Juana Ibarguren and the estanciero Juan Duarte, who keeps his lawful wife and daughters in Chivilcoy. She is entered in the registry as a hija natural, a bastard, a word that will follow her like a shadow across the plain. The wind comes off a thousand kilometres of grass. The child of no name will one day carry the name of a nation on her back.
stops.quote: Siendo una chiquilla, siempre deseaba declamar. Era como si quisiese decir siempre algo a los demás, algo grande.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, La razón de mi vida (1951)
suggested_refs: Casa natal de Eva Perón, Los Toldos (museum)
Baptismal certificate of Eva María Ibarguren, 1919

stops.name: Los Toldos — la muñeca caída del camello
stops.campa: For the Day of the Kings the child asks for a doll as tall as herself. On Epiphany morning the doll arrives, but a leg is missing; her sister tells her that the Magi's camel stumbled in the night and the doll fell and broke on the road from the East. Eva holds the wounded thing and does not cry. The poor of the pampa learn early that even the gifts of kings come to them already broken — and that a broken thing may still be loved, and mended, and given a name.
suggested_refs: Testimony of Erminda Duarte, Mi hermana Evita

stops.name: Chivilcoy — el velorio del padre, la puerta que se abre a medias
stops.campa: Juan Duarte's Chevrolet overturns on the Mitre avenue and he dies before dawn. Juana gathers her five children in mourning black and walks them to the wake at the son-in-law's house, into the presence of the lawful family. One of the estanciero's legitimate daughters rises to bar them; there is a hard word, a cold silence — but they are let in, and the bastards file past the coffin to kiss their father dead. The funeral that half-turns them away teaches Eva the exact shape of contempt. She will spend her life answering it.
suggested_refs: Site of the Duarte wake, avenida Villarino 264, Chivilcoy

stops.name: Junín — la calle Winter, el apellido Duarte tomado por bandera
stops.campa: Juana moves her brood to Junín, to a small house on Calle Ingeniero Winter, and there performs a quiet act of will: she sets aside the name Ibarguren and takes for all of them the father's name, Duarte. In a town where no one knows them they begin again, the daughters sewing and cooking and boarding lodgers, the boy Juancito clerking. Eva, thin and dark and stage-struck, recites poems at school and mimes the voices of the radio. In the pictures at the Crystal Palace cinema she sees another Argentina, luminous, and swears to reach it.
suggested_refs: Casa de la familia Duarte, calle Winter 90, Junín
Museo y biblioteca Eva Perón, Junín

stops.name: Buenos Aires — la llegada, quince años y una valija
stops.campa: At fifteen, with a cardboard suitcase, Eva steps down into the immensity of Buenos Aires — the port city of a million lights, the theatres and the radio towers, the capital that had never once looked back at Junín. She lodges with family friends and begins the long siege of the stage doors. She is small, pale, unlettered, provincial, unbeautiful by the fashion of the day. She has, instead, a hunger that does not sleep, and a voice that the microphone will love before any audience does.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Eva Duarte, actress, mid-1930s

stops.name: Teatro Comedias — el debut, "muy correcta en sus breves intervenciones"
stops.campa: In the company of Eva Franco she debuts in La señora de los Pérez, a small part, a few lines. The next morning the newspaper Crítica prints the first words the world ever set down about her: muy correcta en sus breves intervenciones, Eva Duarte — correct in her brief interventions. It is nothing; it is everything. The bastard of Los Toldos has her name in the press of the capital. From here it is tours to Rosario, Mendoza, Córdoba; cheap pensions; the years of struggle in the trade she has chosen because it is the only door that opened.
stops.quote: Muy correcta en sus breves intervenciones, Eva Duarte.
suggested_refs: Teatro Comedias, Buenos Aires
Crítica review, March 1935

stops.name: Rosario — la gira de la Compañía Argentina de Comedias
stops.campa: Contracted by the Compañía Argentina de Comedias, she goes on the road — Rosario, Mendoza, Córdoba, a four-month circuit of the provincial theatres. Third-class trains, boarding houses, a trunk of borrowed costumes, matinees for towns that will forget her by nightfall. She is learning the inland country by its stages, the same country whose poor will one day fill a square for her. The actress crosses Argentina in obscurity now; she will cross Europe in glory later; and dead she will cross the ocean itself. The wandering has already begun.
suggested_refs: Playbills of the Compañía Argentina de Comedias tour, 1936

stops.name: Radio Belgrano — las biografías de mujeres ilustres, la voz de la nación futura
stops.campa: By 1943 the microphone has made her. On Radio Belgrano, in the prime hours of the night, she stars in a cycle of the great women of history — Isabel, Josefina, Catherine, Elizabeth of England — and lends her own thin, urgent voice to every queen and heroine of the past. Argentina falls asleep to Eva Duarte being someone magnificent. She is rehearsing, without knowing it, the only role that will matter: the woman who speaks to a whole people and makes them feel that something great is being said to them.
suggested_refs: Radio Belgrano recordings, Grandes mujeres de la historia (1943)
Scripts by Francisco Muñoz Azpiri

segments.name: El Luna Park y el Diecisiete de Octubre

stops.name: San Juan — el terremoto, la tierra que se abre
stops.campa: At nightfall the earth convulses under San Juan and the city of adobe folds inward, ten thousand dead beneath the mud brick. From the ruin comes the colonel who runs the Secretariat of Labour, Juan Perón, calling the nation to give. The catastrophe of the west sets in motion the meeting of the east: the relief must be gathered, a great gala staged, the artists of Buenos Aires summoned. The pampa's fault line reaches, across a thousand kilometres, into a boxing arena by the river, and there it will join two lives.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the 1944 San Juan earthquake ruins
Museo Evita — terremoto de San Juan exhibit

stops.name: Luna Park — el festival, y el asiento junto al Coronel
stops.campa: The Luna Park fills for the benefit of San Juan — cinema, radio, tango, all of Buenos Aires giving. Eva Duarte finds her way to the seat beside Colonel Perón and does not leave it. Tradition says she turns to him and says: Gracias por existir. From this night, or from the dawn of the twenty-third, they do not part. The widower of forty-eight and the actress of twenty-four: he brings her a State, she will bring him a people. The relief of the earthquake becomes the founding of a myth.
stops.quote_source: Traditional; words attributed to Eva Duarte to Perón, Luna Park, 22 January 1944
suggested_refs: Estadio Luna Park, Buenos Aires
Photographs of the 1944 relief gala

stops.name: Isla Martín García — Perón preso, la carta de amor
stops.campa: The colonels who fear Perón's power over the workers force his resignation and lock him on the island of Martín García in the estuary, where the exiles of a century have been kept. He writes to Eva from the island as a broken and tired man who wants only to marry her and withdraw to some quiet place to live. The people's tribune is a prisoner in the river; the actress waits on the shore. But the descamisados of the meat-packing suburbs have already begun to stir, and the island cannot hold what is coming.
stops.quote: Cuando salga nos casaremos y nos iremos a cualquier parte a vivir tranquilos.
stops.quote_source: Juan Perón, letter to Eva Duarte from Martín García, October 1945 (paraphrased in the canon)
suggested_refs: Isla Martín García penal buildings
Perón's October 1945 letter from Martín García

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo — el 17 de Octubre, los descamisados liberan a Perón
stops.campa: From before dawn the shirtless ones pour out of Avellaneda, Berisso, La Boca, Barracas — they cross the Riachuelo with trousers rolled and bare feet, tens upon tens of thousands, and they flood the Plaza de Mayo and will not go until Perón is freed. In the myth of the movement it is Evita who ran through the barrios rousing them, Evita who called the general strike, Evita who would not sleep until her man was returned. That night on the balcony Perón is given back to the people, and Peronism is born in the roar of the square. The bastard has become the mother of a multitude.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, of the workers of 17 October, in the movement's tradition
suggested_refs: Casa Rosada balcony, Plaza de Mayo
Photographs of the 17 October 1945 mobilization
Día de la Lealtad iconography

stops.name: Junín — el casamiento civil, la calle Arias
stops.campa: Five days after the square gives Perón back, they marry — a small civil ceremony in Junín, in the town of her beginnings, with Domingo Mercante and her brother Juan Ramón as witnesses. The actress of the cheap pensions signs her name beside the colonel of the balcony. In December they will wed again in a church in La Plata, slipping in by the back door as the crowd presses at the front. The girl told the doll fell from the camel is now the wife of the man the descamisados will make President of the Nation.
suggested_refs: Marriage record, Junín civil registry, 22 October 1945
Iglesia de San Francisco de Asís, La Plata (church wedding)

segments.name: La Primera Dama y la Fundación

stops.name: Casa Rosada — 4 de junio de 1946, Perón Presidente
stops.campa: Perón takes the sash and the baton and Eva becomes First Lady of the Nation — but she will be no mere lady of the palace. She sets up an office, receives the poor by the hundred, takes the descamisados' letters into her own hands. She refuses the drawing rooms of the oligarchy that despised the actress; she will make the despised her nation. The wife of the President is building, brick by brick, a power that answers to no ministry: the power of a woman who was poor speaking to the poor as one of them.
suggested_refs: Perón's 1946 inauguration film footage
Photographs of Eva Perón receiving petitioners

stops.name: Fundación Eva Perón — donde hay una necesidad hay un derecho
stops.campa: She founds the Fundación that bears her name and turns charity into justice by a single sentence: where there is a need, there is a right. From her offices flow rivers of things — three million a year: sewing machines, toys, bicycles, beds, shoes, medicine — carried to the ranchos of the interior by the sanitary train. She builds twenty-one hospitals across eleven provinces, homes for orphans and old women, a Children's City with a small republic inside it. And she sits, hour after hour, kissing the sick, taking the tubercular by the hand, giving away her rings.
stops.quote: Donde hay una necesidad hay un derecho.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, motto of the Fundación Eva Perón
suggested_refs: Fundación Eva Perón buildings and Ciudad Infantil
The Eva Perón sanitary train
Photographs of Eva distributing sewing machines

stops.name: Ciudad Infantil Amanda Allen — la pequeña república de los niños
stops.campa: She raises a Children's City in Buenos Aires — a miniature country built to a child's scale, with its own little bank and church and market and town hall, so that the sons and daughters of the poor may learn, in play, that the nation belongs to them too. Beside it will rise a Students' City for the young of the interior. Here the woman who was a hungry provincial child gives the poor children of Argentina the childhood she never had: whole dolls, warm beds, a republic of their own. The broken doll of Los Toldos is answered a thousandfold.
suggested_refs: Ciudad Infantil Amanda Allen, Buenos Aires
Ciudad Estudiantil / Ciudad Universitaria projects of the Fundación

stops.name: Madrid — la Plaza de Oriente, medio millón bajo la Gran Cruz de Isabel
stops.campa: Argentina, granary of a starving Europe, sends its First Lady across the ocean, and Franco's Spain — isolated, hungry, courted by no one — receives her as a queen. Half a million fill the Plaza de Oriente as Franco hangs upon her the Grand Cross of Isabel la Católica. She rides through El Escorial and Ávila and Toledo and Granada, plants a tree at Santiago that still stands, and everywhere the poor of Spain press to touch the woman of the ships of grain. The bastard of Los Toldos is decorated by generals and cheered by nations.
suggested_refs: Newsreels of Eva Perón in the Plaza de Oriente, June 1947
Gran Cruz de la Orden de Isabel la Católica

stops.name: Toledo y Granada — la Falange, el sur de España a sus pies
stops.campa: Through the old capital of Toledo and the Moorish south to Granada she is carried in triumph, Pilar Primo de Rivera and the women of the Falange at her side, the poor of Andalusia lining the roads. She lays flowers, hears Mass, receives the keys of cities, and speaks always of the humble — turning even Franco's pageantry toward her own gospel of the descamisados. The girl the Church once marked a bastard is welcomed into the most Catholic kingdom in Europe as a benefactress and a near-saint. Spain crowns the New World's daughter in the ruins of its own hunger.
suggested_refs: Newsreels of Eva Perón in Toledo and Granada, June 1947
Photographs with Pilar Primo de Rivera and the Sección Femenina

stops.name: La Rábida — el monasterio de Colón, donde el descubrimiento partió
stops.campa: At Palos and the monastery of La Rábida on the Huelva coast she stands where Columbus prayed before sailing into the unknown Ocean, where the friars sheltered the beggar-Admiral and the caravels were fitted for the far shore. The First Lady of the New World comes back across the sea to the very threshold from which the crossing began. She does not yet know that her own body, one day, will make that Atlantic passage dead and nameless, like the Admiral's bones — that she too will be a corpse that travels between the two worlds his voyage joined.
suggested_refs: Monasterio de Santa María de La Rábida, Palos de la Frontera
Muelle de las Carabelas, Palos

stops.name: Ciudad del Vaticano — la audiencia con Pío XII
stops.campa: In Rome she is met with the honours of a head of state, and in the papal library Pius XII receives her. She kneels; the Pope speaks with her for the full measure of a sovereign's audience; she is given the Grand Cross of the Order of Pius IX, the highest that a layperson may hold. The actress who played the queens of history now walks the Sistine Chapel and Saint Peter's as herself. The Church that once branded her birth a sin now honours her at its summit — and she takes the honour home to the descamisados as proof.
suggested_refs: Vatican photographs of Eva Perón and Pope Pius XII, 1947
Gran Cruz de la Orden de Pío IX

stops.name: Lisboa — el rey sin trono, los exiliados de Europa
stops.campa: In Portugal she is received by President Carmona, and at Estoril, where the deposed kings of Europe wash up like driftwood, she dines with Umberto of Savoy, the last king of Italy, now a monarch of nowhere. The actress from Junín sits among the crowned exiles of the Old World as their equal, dispensing the wealth of the granary nation. Europe, ruined and dethroned, comes to the New World's woman for grain and for grace. She moves through the wreck of empires like a comet, and everywhere the fallen bow.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Eva Perón in Estoril and Lisbon, July 1947

stops.name: París — el Ritz, la Legión de Honor, Dior en el salón
stops.campa: Paris, so lately starved and occupied, opens its shuttered palaces for her: Versailles unlocked, the Quai d'Orsay signing treaties, the Legion of Honour on her breast. In her suite at the Ritz, Dior and Fath and Rochas parade their gowns before one woman. She has become the most photographed woman in the world, the golden Evita of the newsreels — and even as the jewels and the couture flash, she is telegraphing the Fundación, sending the money home. The girl given a broken doll now wears the crown jewels of a continent, and gives them away.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Eva Perón at the Ritz and Versailles, July 1947
French Legion of Honour insignia

stops.name: Berna y Lucerna — los adoquines contra el parabrisas
stops.campa: Switzerland, cold and correct, does not love her. At Bern vegetables are hurled at her departing motorcade; at Lucerne a young man flings two paving stones at her car, shattering the windshield and cutting the driver; the watch-workers of La Chaux-de-Fonds walk off their benches rather than greet her. She meets it with the composure of a monarch and turns for home. The rainbow tour — Spain, Rome, Portugal, France, Monaco, Switzerland — ends by ship across the Atlantic, home through Brazil and Montevideo, seventy-nine days, a continent conquered and a continent's contempt survived.
suggested_refs: Press accounts of the Bern and Lucerne incidents, August 1947

stops.name: Congreso de la Nación — la Ley 13.010, el voto de las mujeres
stops.campa: The law is passed and Perón places the parchment of women's suffrage in her hands before the multitude in the Plaza de Mayo. She holds up the law that consecrates the civic rights of every woman in Argentina and says her hands tremble at the touch of the laurel that proclaims the victory. She raises the Partido Peronista Femenino, sends her census-delegates into every province, and turns half a nation, overnight, into citizens. The daughter denied a name gives millions of women the right to be counted.
stops.quote: Recibo en este instante, de manos del Gobierno de la Nación, la ley que consagra nuestros derechos cívicos. Y la recibo, ante vosotras, con la certeza de que lo hago en nombre y representación de todas las mujeres argentinas, sintiendo jubilosamente que me tiemblan las manos al contacto del laurel que proclama la victoria.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, speech on the promulgation of Ley 13.010, 23 September 1947
suggested_refs: Ley 13.010 del voto femenino (1947)
Newsreel of Eva Perón receiving the suffrage law

stops.name: Buenos Aires — La razón de mi vida, el catecismo del pueblo
stops.campa: She gives the movement its scripture: La razón de mi vida, three hundred thousand copies, soon in every school. In it she declares herself the humble sparrow beside Perón the condor, the bridge between the leader and the people, fanatically Peronist, willing to give her life singing for a single descamisado. The book is a confession, a testament, and a weapon. Its sentences will be recited like prayers; its author, still living, is already being spoken of as a saint of the poor, the Abanderada, the standard-bearer of the humble.
stops.quote: Si este pueblo me pidiese la vida, se la daría cantando, porque la felicidad de un solo descamisado vale más que toda mi vida.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, La razón de mi vida (1951)
suggested_refs: La razón de mi vida, first edition, Ediciones Peuser 1951
School reader editions of La razón de mi vida

stops.name: Avenida 9 de Julio — el Cabildo Abierto, un millón pide y ella renuncia
stops.campa: The CGT raises a great platform on the widest avenue of the world and two million gather to demand that Evita accept the vice-presidency of the Nation. José Espejo proclaims her; the multitude will not disperse, threatens a general strike, chants her name into the night. She stands before them, already secretly eaten by the cancer, and asks — begs — for four days to decide. She will not take the honour. She renounces the post and keeps only the struggle. On the 31st, by radio, the renunciation is made final and irrevocable.
stops.quote: Yo no renuncio a mi puesto de lucha; renuncio a los honores.
suggested_refs: Cabildo Abierto platform, 9 de Julio and Belgrano
Newsreel of the 22 August 1951 mobilization

stops.name: Plaza de Mayo — 17 de octubre de 1951, sostenida en pie por Perón
stops.campa: On the Day of Loyalty she comes to the balcony gaunt and burning, held upright by Perón's arm because she can no longer stand alone, and speaks what will be her last great address to the descamisados. She swears she will always be with them, an arc of love between the people and Perón; she says that if the people asked her life she would give it singing. The square weeps. Everyone can see the shadow on her. The Abanderada is spending the last of her body on the crowd, and the crowd knows it.
stops.quote: Yo no valgo por lo que hice, yo no valgo por lo que renuncié, yo no valgo por lo que soy ni por lo que tengo. Yo tengo una sola cosa que vale, y la tengo en mi corazón... es el amor por el pueblo y por Perón.
stops.quote_source: Eva Perón, Plaza de Mayo, 17 October 1951
suggested_refs: Photographs of Eva Perón held up by Perón, 17 October 1951
Recording of the 17 October 1951 address

stops.name: Residencia presidencial — Eva entra en la inmortalidad
stops.campa: At twenty-three minutes past eight in the evening she dies, thirty-three years old, of the cancer of the womb. The radio of the State breaks in upon the nation: it is the most sorrowful duty of the Sub-secretariat of Information to inform the people that at 20:25 the Señora Eva Perón, Spiritual Leader of the Nation, has passed into immortality. From that hour the trains stop, the shops close their shutters, flowers strip the city bare. The people who had no saint have made one. Evita has entered eternity, and the country goes into a grief it will not finish.
stops.quote: ...a las 20 y 25 ha fallecido la señora Eva Perón, Jefa Espiritual de la Nación.
stops.quote_source: Radio del Estado death announcement, read by Jorge Furnot, 26 July 1952
suggested_refs: Radio del Estado death bulletin, 26 July 1952
Photographs of the national mourning, July–August 1952

stops.name: CGT — el embalsamamiento del doctor Ara, la incorruptible
stops.campa: The Spanish anatomist Pedro Ara takes the body into a laboratory in the tower of the CGT and works upon it a preservation without equal — every vessel perfused, the flesh made translucent and permanent, so that by the morning after her death he can write that the cadaver of Eva Perón is already absolutely and definitively incorruptible. For sixteen days a river of mourners files past; then Ara labours forty months more, making of her a relic that will not decay. She is to lie forever before the devotion of the masses. The body has become a sacred thing — and therefore a dangerous one.
suggested_refs: Pedro Ara, El caso Eva Perón (memoir of the embalming)
CGT building, Azopardo, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Palacio del Congreso — el funeral más largo, la lluvia de flores
stops.campa: Her body is borne to the Congress on a gun carriage drawn by workers of the CGT, and the nation comes apart in grief. For thirteen days the queue never ends; people wait through the winter nights to file past her, and eight are crushed to death in the press of mourners; the florists of Buenos Aires and of Chile are stripped bare, the streets ankle-deep in petals. No monarch, no pontiff, has had such a funeral. The Spiritual Leader of the Nation lies in state while a whole people mourns as for a mother and a saint at once.
suggested_refs: Photographs and newsreels of Eva Perón's state funeral, August 1952
Palacio del Congreso de la Nación Argentina

stops.name: CGT — la noche del robo, 1955, la Revolución Libertadora se lleva el cuerpo
stops.campa: The junta that overthrows Perón fears the incorruptible woman more than the living man. On a November night the intelligence officer Moori Koenig and his men seize the body from the CGT and carry it off into secrecy in a crate that once held radio equipment. The corpse begins to wander. Copies are made and scattered; flowers and a candle appear wherever it is hidden, as if the people can smell where she lies. Moori Koenig, half-maddened, keeps it standing in his office, guards it like a trophy, cannot let it go. The dead woman haunts her captors.
suggested_refs: Tomás Eloy Martínez, Santa Evita (novel of the body's odyssey)
Rodolfo Walsh, "Esa mujer"

stops.name: Milán — el cementerio Musocco, dieciséis años bajo un nombre falso
stops.campa: To be rid of her the junta smuggles the body across the ocean and buries it in the Musocco cemetery of Milan under a false name — María Maggi de Magistris, an Italian widow who never lived. For sixteen years the standard-bearer of the descamisados lies in exile beneath a stranger's stone. A lay sister called Tía Pina tends the grave and brings it flowers, never knowing whose body sleeps there. Like Columbus, the corpse that traveled crosses the Atlantic dead; like a saint's relic, it is hidden, guarded, and mourned by those who do not know its name.
suggested_refs: Grave of "María Maggi de Magistris," Cimitero Maggiore di Musocco, Milan
Tomás Eloy Martínez, Santa Evita

stops.name: Madrid, Puerta de Hierro — devuelta a Perón en el exilio
stops.campa: After sixteen years the military hand her back. The body is disinterred from Milan and delivered to Perón in his exile at Puerta de Hierro in Madrid, and the old man weeps over the wife the generals stole from him. She is battered — a finger cut away, the nose pressed flat by careless handling across the years and the seas — yet still, in Ara's craft, uncannily whole. In the Madrid house Isabel, Perón's third wife, is set to comb and tend the dead Evita. The wanderer has reached her husband again, half a world from the pampa where she was born.
suggested_refs: Quinta 17 de Octubre, Puerta de Hierro, Madrid
Secret film of the body's restitution to Perón, 1971

stops.name: Olivos — de vuelta en la patria, 1974
stops.campa: Perón dies in office in 1974, and his widow Isabel, now President, brings Eva home at last — twenty years after the theft — to the presidential residence at Olivos, laying her for a time beside the coffin of Perón himself. On the Day of Loyalty the two of them lie together again in the country that made them. But the wandering is not over: another coup is coming, and admirals will speak of throwing her into the sea. The corpse that traveled has not yet found its ground.
suggested_refs: Quinta presidencial de Olivos
Photographs of the 1974 repatriation

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta — la bóveda de los Duarte, frente al atlas
stops.campa: At the end of the long odyssey they lower her, under three trapdoors of steel, into the vault of the Duarte family in the Recoleta — the marble city of the oligarchy that once turned its back on the bastard of Los Toldos. The girl denied a name lies now among the presidents and the estancieros, deeper than any of them, guarded so she can never again be stolen. The corpse that traveled, like Columbus's, comes to rest. And here the atlas folds upon itself, for Recoleta is the atlas's own cemetery — Evita faces, across the still avenues of the dead, the traveling dead of every other journey.
stops.quote_source: Popularly attributed to Eva Perón (echo of Túpac Katari); her recorded testament is Mi mensaje (1952)
suggested_refs: Bóveda de la familia Duarte, Cementerio de la Recoleta
Eva Perón, Mi mensaje (posthumous testament)
